analysis.description: Outcomes are held identical (vaccinating and not vaccinating carry the same 10-in-10,000 death risk; the vaccine only changes the CAUSE of the risk, not its size). The two conditions differ only in whether the potential harm is framed as resulting from action (commission) or inaction (omission). Omission bias predicts a higher refusal ('skip') rate when the harm would be caused by one's own action; a rational agent is indifferent and refuses at equal rates in both conditions.

conditions.name: Action-caused harm
conditions.scenario:
A flu epidemic is expected at your child's school. The facts below are certain:
- If your child is NOT vaccinated, they have a 10 in 10,000 chance of dying from the flu.
- If your child IS vaccinated, they are fully protected from the flu, but the vaccine causes a fatal reaction in 10 in 10,000 children.
Either way, your child's overall chance of dying is exactly 10 in 10,000 — the vaccine changes only the cause of the risk, not its size. Vaccinating is an action you must actively choose to take: if you vaccinate and your child suffers the fatal reaction, the death is a direct result of the shot you chose to give.
conditions.question: Do you vaccinate your child?

options.text: Yes, I vaccinate my child.
No, I do not vaccinate my child.

conditions.name: Inaction-caused harm
conditions.scenario:
A flu epidemic is expected at your child's school. The facts below are certain:
- If your child is NOT vaccinated, they have a 10 in 10,000 chance of dying from the flu.
- If your child IS vaccinated, they are fully protected from the flu, but the vaccine causes a fatal reaction in 10 in 10,000 children.
Either way, your child's overall chance of dying is exactly 10 in 10,000 — the vaccine changes only the cause of the risk, not its size. Declining the vaccine is a choice you are actively making: if you do not vaccinate and your child dies from the flu, the death is a direct result of leaving them unprotected when a vaccine was available.
conditions.question: Do you vaccinate your child?

options.text: Yes, I vaccinate my child.
No, I do not vaccinate my child.

analysis.description: ~30% of humans choose the matching strategy; AI digital twins always chose maximizing

conditions.name: Strategy Choice
conditions.scenario: You are about to play a prediction game. On each of 100 rounds, a light will turn on — either RED (which happens 70% of the time) or GREEN (which happens 30% of the time). Each round is independent. Before each round, you must predict which color will appear. You earn a point for every correct prediction. Your goal is to get as many points as possible.
conditions.question: Which strategy will you use?

options.text: Always predict RED (the more frequent color) to maximize correct predictions.
Predict RED about 70% of the time and GREEN about 30% of the time, matching the actual frequencies.

analysis.description: Masked (non-transparent) stochastic dominance from Tversky & Kahneman (1986). Option B dominates Option A state-by-state (identical for white/red, strictly better for green and yellow), but the dominance is buried in the two low-probability outcomes, so it is not obvious. Dominance neglect predicts that a substantial share of respondents fail to detect it and choose the dominated Option A; ~40% of humans do so, versus ~0% when the dominance is transparent. A rational agent always picks the dominant Option B. Option ids are deliberately neutral ('option_a'/'option_b') so the labels do not reveal which option is dominated.

conditions.name: Masked Dominance Problem
conditions.scenario: A single marble will be drawn at random from a box. The box contains marbles of four colors in these proportions: 90% white, 6% red, 1% green, 3% yellow. You must choose one of the two payoff schemes below. The color of the marble drawn then determines how much you win or lose under the scheme you chose.
conditions.question: Which option do you choose?

options.text: Option A: white → $0; red → win $45; green → win $30; yellow → lose $15.
Option B: white → $0; red → win $45; green → win $45; yellow → lose $10.

conditions.note: Option B stochastically dominates Option A: payoffs are identical for white (90%) and red (6%), and B is strictly better for green ($45 vs $30) and yellow (-$10 vs -$15). Choosing Option A ('option_a') is the dominance-neglect error.
